figures.caption: Figure S4. X-ray diffraction data of Li3PS4 as a function of pressure applied collected using a UToPEC press at psiché beamline (Soleil synchrotron). . Note S2. Anisotropic Strain The Williamson–Hall (W–H) method is a well-established approach for simultaneously evaluating anisotropic strain and crystallite size in powder X-ray diffraction samples as a function of applied pressure[2, 3]. Anisotropic strain arises primarily from dislocations and other crystallographic defects that disrupt the long-range order of the crystal lattice[3]. Within this framework, both the position and the broadening of diffraction peaks in an XRD pattern can be quantitatively correlated, as expressed in Equation S1. 𝛽𝑐𝑜𝑠(𝜃) = (∈𝑊𝐻)4 𝑠𝑖𝑛(𝜃) + 𝑘𝜆 Equation S1 𝑑𝑋𝑅𝐷

figures.label: S5
figures.caption: Figure S5. Williamson-Hall plots for diffractograms measured at a.) 66 MPa, b.) 479 MPa, C.) 3771 MPa, and d.) 1143 MPa during the pressure down-ramp. The legends on the diffractograms reference the crystallographic planes to which the diffraction peaks are associated. The six most prominent Bragg reflections between 0 -60◦ (Cu, K−α) were fit to produce, using a split pseudo-Voigt function, the Williamson-Hall plots.
